game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
10/10 Drag and drop simulator.

The game sounded really interesting but after 2 hours of playtime I refunded it. The idea that you hunt for information and decide what to pass on and what to keep private is a nice way of turning a game into a subtle reference to personal bias. A clever idea that could have been great. The problem is that, certainly for the 2 hours I played, that simply wasn't the case. There is no hunting for information. It is handed to you on a plate. The basic routine is this:

A page of information is loaded and appears on the right of the screen. Important parts of the text are highlighted. Click the highlighted text and drag it to the Orwell upload facility on the left of the screen. Drag enough pieces of text and a new page of information is presented to you with highlighted parts. Drag and drop. New page. Drag and drop. New page.

You will discover social media handles. Great, now you can hunt the person down and..oh wait, no their feed just gets presented to you with highlighted text. Drag and drop.

You manage to get the telephone number of a suspect. Now you can tap their line and listen in on their conversations. Oh wait, it just gets presented to you, no action required. Never mind, look, there's the symbol to say they are about to have a conversation. QUICK, check in and listen to them before they...oh wait, no. You can simply ignore the symbol for half an hour and then check it, because the messages only start when you open up the screen. If these really are terrorists, they are the most considerate ones on the planet as they refuse to start their conversation until you are listening in. Try to keep up? No need, go make a drink, come back and find the page of text. Ignore the drivel, the important bits are highlighted.  Drag and drop.

Still, your decisions about what to upload is really what the game is about. Except that even in those first 2 hours there were a few occasions where I decided not to upload something because it appeared to be out of context. A message displaying agressiveness or hatred of the state, but in the context of the document it seemed to be just social media waffle and not really genuine terrorist. So I didn't upload it. Result? Nothing. The game simply wouldn't progress until I uploaded it. The choice was removed. So after a while of hunting and finding no new clues I reluctantly uploaded the info and lo and behold a new page of information was presented to me. Drag and drop. Rinse and repeat.

Clearly a lot of people have found something great in this game and I truly love the concept but I cannot recommend it for what it claims to be.  If you are looking for the perfect Drag and Drop Simulator to spend your evenings on though, you can't go wrong here.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Disappointing.  

1. Incredibly short.  I was surprised when it was over, as it felt like I just completed a tutorial.
2. Hand holding the entire way through.  Your "adviser" or "controller" does just that, controls you.  All you do is drag and drop things.  You make very few decisions and are spoon fed what you need to do next.
3. Worse than number 2, you are spoon fed what to think and make of your findings.  Rather than allowing you to actually investigate and figure things out, the game tells you precisely what to think.  This kills immersion and makes you, not an investigator, but just a peon dragging and dropping lines of text.
4. Game locked up for me on conclusion.  I have only played through one ending and have no desire to do the others, because the gameplay is like a tutorial from start to finish.  It would be tedious as hell playing through it again.
5. Writing is corny.  It feels like it is forcing the dialogue to be edgy and using memes.  Seriously feels like an awful episode of BBT.

So much potential, but fails the entire way through.  Definitely not worth 10 pounds.  Not even worth 5.  Maybe 1.99.  The game is incredibly short.  Steam says I played it for 7.1 hours, but the reality is I fell asleep while playing about halfway through and dozed off for a couple hours.  Even at 7 hours, the gameplay is disappointingly short.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wish I liked it because on the paper it's 100% a game for me but I'm forced to admit I just don't.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" seems content to repeat what books and movies have said more eloquently.  It also falls below the dollar per hour metric (it can be completed within 5 hours).

The gameplay is simple and involves clicking through fake internet websites, blogs, and chat logs to collect bits of information (a process that can easily become tedious).

So the appeal is obviously the story, but for $9.99, you're better off buying a copy of George Orwell's 1984, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World instead. This game is nothing more than a shallow summary of the themes explored in depth by those literary works.

Unity engine build: 2018.3.0f2. There were some graphical issues with the native Linux version. Solved by using Proton.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: great game buggered by stupid save system. 

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell to my comprehension is a game set in Britain, being in a timeline where camera's and invasive technology are being ushered in by the government, under the guise of safety. The game's premise, location and the name itself draw distinct premise to a book, written by an individual who fought the Spaniards in the 20th century. The man had other notable accomplishments, such as wrestling adult elephants in front of rural Indian villagers, as a gesture of the might of Great Britian. In essence, it is inherently blatant that this idea being presented in Orwell is exceptionally intriguing, however, it all turns awry. 

What I have had to endure is worse than potential intrusion and subsequent sexual depravity at the government, Orwell is none other than a point and click adventure game. Woe and despair have betided me, for In the history of fabled lore, no successful game has abided by a point and click adventure structure, it is inherently a recipe for disaster, one that only lunatics and fiends will attempt to pursue. However, due to my own altruistic merit, I attempted engage and judge Orwell in an impartial way, albeit I remained wary. Within time, it became clear that my fears were correct. In a game of this calibre dialogue or the development of the ambience becomes imperative, however, unfortunately this game was the opposite. On numerous occasions I encountered various fallacies in Orwell's writing, for example they stated "Mom" as opposed to the genuine spelling in Britain, that is "Mum". Alongside this trivial mistake, the rest of the dialogue is utterly obsolete, with the intel being utterly repetitive and tedious, having no distinctive effect on the genuine flow of the game. This affirms my belief that the armies of Tartarus have escaped their confinement and harnassed the power of the internet, attempting to conduct a period of psychological warfare upon their adversaries, which just so happen to be the denizens of Steam. Likely, you are currently contemplating that I am exaggerating, being prone to drama or embellishment, in preparation of this event I summarised a portion of the dialogue, certifying my analysis. The first individual stated, "Hey can you bomb this square for me?", with the other responding, "I don't want to commit a terrorist attack". This statement was then countered by the resolute, "Awww, I baked muffins.", following by the individual relenting and going, "Bah, you discovered my weakness, fine ill do it." It is a rare circumstance that I feel the necessity to go on a blood curling massacre, reaping havoc upon the local populace, however, after witnessing this peculiar exchange in game I allowed myself the luxury. It is completely baffling how an innocuous, benign statement regarding muffins can be used to convince an individual into committing a terrorist attack, the writers have had their minds completely distorted of all forms of sanity, leaving an unhinged, muffin crazed remnant of a mind to remain. The ludicrousness of the writing then conveniently places an entrance into the other main gripe, the character interactions. The characters continuously, throughout the game converse in the most inhuman fashion I have ever encountered, every attempt at conversation is filled to the brim with various Emoji's, faces concocted out of text and abbreviations that produce an incoherent spiralled mess. This then raises complications, as some of the characters are supposed professional writers, working for reputable news company. This conflicts with their genuine writing style however, which appears filled to the brim with profanity, grammatical errors and a blatant attempt at attempting to mimic the stereotypical view that I assume millennial's believe, regarding today's youth. All in all the writers, to my analysis are simultaneously both socially and linguistically inept. While I can completely comprehend the fact that the writers are likely forced to induce semen daily, tortured after falling asleep on their 20 hour shift and are likely in solitude, away from any form of sentient life away from the workplace, it still bears no excuse to the shoddily, artificial dialogue. On a game so reliant on literature and character interaction, it falls abruptly into an expertly crafted brick wall. review_text_raw:
Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a "profession simulator" style interactive novel where you control a privacy invading government employee, reading peoples emails and watching security cameras.  You're forced to make decisions to progress the story, although in a bit of hamfisted design, the developers obscure a lot of the readily available information you would have just to make the game more "interesting". 

The game is a very dry computer operation simulator where you're stuck using a fake web browser to plod through the tedious game, copying text and clicking on this and that.   I'm sure there's a "watching paint dry" simulator on Steam and it would be just as engaging.  Bonus points for the sheer irony of a game about big brother asking you for your email address so they can spam you and collect data on you.  That kind of dodginess is completely reprehensible, so even if the game was actually any good, I still wouldn't recommend it to make sure the developers are getting the message.

review_text_raw:
I bought this game with the surveillance pack while it was on sale, and boy do I regret it. This game has a fun idea, but that's about it.

First, the gameplay is very disappointing and tiring. You don't have to look for anything, as everything is highlighted. There are few choices, and you only need to click and drag on the side. Every time you put a clue into the "database," you get interrupted by a guy either mocking you for adding an "useless" piece of information or explaining what you just added and how it helps in the story line. You can never be wrong putting a clue because you get corrected or the guy confirms that the clue is correct and explains it, it just feels like you're on a tutorial mode the entire game. Also, the fact that you can't change the clues you added or erase them is a pain. You can prevent that by hovering over a clue to see what it will add, but I didn't know that because this game bugged so much that the information didn't appear until mid-game.

The story is simple and I found it okay. It has some plot twists, etc., but it is very long for its worth. There are multiple endings, and just to get one is very confusing because it feels like every possible ending is being thrown at you and you have to pick one. I already forced myself to finish one, and I don't think I will launch this game again.

Overall, if you're looking for a small investigation game or want to feel like a detective, pass on this game. It would have been a great mobile game, but is tedious on PC.

To show you how bad I felt playing this, this is my first review I have ever made. It's not that I didn't like the game; I really [u][i]disliked[/i][/u] it and forced my way until the end.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

- Engaging ethical themes and dilemmas
- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

At first I was enthralled. They built a small universe that was only a hop, skip, and step away from the one I'm familiar with (good ol' US of A), and I was immediately taken in. I went through the first episode dutifully following along, reading everything I could get my hands on in the game. I combed through the info and made sure the data I supplied was tip-top. I finished out the first day (level) and felt good. Then the second day started.

It was the same thing, except I had a couple other targets to watch. I felt like I had already exhausted the gameplay. Find highlighted text, decide whether or not you want it, drag to box. Occasionally switch box from one character to another (which really just become pedantic when you end up only dealing with five or so interconnected characters). There's no real risk unless you just mean to do poorly, if its even possible. You can't really miss anything, so you never have to juggle the lives of all your surveillance targets. Their web-entries, conversation over text and "phone calls" (just more text doesn't read like a real conversation), will patiently wait for you while you sift through all of it. It gets to the point where you're just hunting highlighted words, as if Orwell has already solved the case on its own. Overall, the game is a bit of a dissappointment, which I only finished to see how the story unfolds. You get a few choices, but there is little in the way of making you feel like you had an impact unless you really got into the story.

TL:DR: All in all, the game is repetitive and after playing through the first episode, I really couldn't recommend purchasing the second one unless you really want to continue the story. I can tell the game was a labor of love, but it just doesn't offer any truly unique insights into the surveillance state and the ethical considerations that surround it, let alone the gameplay.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.
